_source.displaydescription:
Cī Bāhāḥ Nani is located to the east of the street that runs from Cyāsala to Olakhu. It is known as Ci Bāhāḥ Libi (a courtyard with a caitya) amongt the local residents. The main facade of the structure has two columns that support a door screen between them. The door has a toraṇa above it and a metal screen to protect the image housed inside the sanctum. The roof has a plastered coping on the boundary wall and a small pinnacle. A cornice band runs along the boundary wall. Although Nanis are often associated with their main Bāhāḥs, this Nani has no association with any other major Bāhāḥ. It solely belongs to the Prajāpati family. Locke (1985, 72) assumes that Nani's present shrine was constructed after the 1934 earthquake. The shrine lacks many major features that are typical to a bāhāḥ.

The main shrine is attached to a boundary wall on the south. The sanctum holds a north-facing stone statue of Akṣobhya wearing a lhegā (metal attire). Following the theft of the original statue a few years ago, this new statue is now protected by a metal grill. Broken pieces of glass have been embedded in the boundary wall for further protection. Above the door, one can find a toraṇa with a lotus petal in its centre. A stone relief depicting the Five Buddhas is placed underneath the image of Akṣobhya. The inscription on the pedestal of these images is now illegible. Images of Nārāyaṇa, Vajradhara, Mañjuśrī, Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla have been placed in a line on the wall. Outside, a Śikharakūṭa Caitya sits in front of the main shrine. The courtyard is paved with concrete tiles. The earliest inscription mentioning this Nani is dated to NS 796.

_source.displaydescription:
Taḥdhãlibi Bāhāḥ can be accessed via a narrow alleyway that runs underneath a residential house, to the north of the way from Uku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260) to Ubāhā Bahī (LAL2280). The main shrine of the bāhāḥ is a plastered structure that is raised above the ground on a plinth. The roof of the temple has a stūpa as its finial, and the temple structure itself is decorated with pilasters at each corner. The main sanctum faces west, and its entrance is emphasised by the triangular motif that sits above it. A small dharmadhātu maṇḍala (45 cm high) and a vajradhātu caitya (145 cm high) that sits on a square base of 120 cm are both lined up centrally to the west of the main shrine. This ensemble of monuments can be found towards the south-eastern corner of the courtyard. The courtyard measures 11.7 m × 9.2 m and is paved in telia tiles. A narrow alley to the north-western corner leads on to the Dune Bāhāḥ (LAL2300).

Generally, this place is not referred to as a bāhāḥ; instead, local residents call it a libi/coka (courtyard). Locke (1985) also does not include this monument in his list of vihāras. However, Śākya (1994, 117-18) counts it as a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260). The structure of this vihāra differs from that of other vihāras. A cement-plastered shrine topped with a stūpa-shaped pinnacle stands on the eastern side of the courtyard. There are no traditional carvings nor decorative objects in this shrine. Nāmasaṅgīti is enshrined in the sanctum as the main deity, and images of Mahākāla and Gaṇeśa have been attached respectively to the northern and the southern walls of the shrine. The shrine can be circumambulated via a narrow passage. 

A largely effaced stone inscription stands at the southeast corner of the caitya. Śākya (1994, 117-18) has identified the date of the inscription as NS 718. However, the inscription is now mostly illegible and so the date could not be confirmed.

This small courtyard, known as Ikhālakhu Bāhāḥ, is located to the east of Ikhālakhu coka. The courtyard is behind a row of residential buildings near the Ikhālakhu Jahru. It is paved with stone flooring.

This small courtyard is located to the east of Ikhālakhu and can be reached through a narrow alley. Measuring 6.5m x 3.75m, it consists of a raised plinth on the northern wall containing three small statues with stone roofs, atop of which are small stupas. At the center is a śikharakūṭa caitya with a base measuring 140 x 140 cm and a height of 170 cm. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala (90 cm tall) adjoins it on its northern side. A small caitya (70cm tall) can be found on the southern plinth attached to the building, and appears to be in a neglected state. A bell hangs on two stone pillars (13 x 13 cm and 170 cm high) to the east of the courtyard.

This tiny courtyard reaches the minimum requirements for a Bāhāḥ as defined by Locke. Bruce Owens notes that the kwāḥpāḥ dyaḥ, caitya, and other features are under threat as this space has been used to store lumber (and now detritus from the reconstruction) since at least 2008. Indeed, most of the features generally found in a vihāra cannot be found here. There is, for instance, no god-house (dyaḥchẽ). Local people therefore consider this place to just be a coka rather than a vihāra.

Three south-facing and connected shrines house the main deities of the vihāra. When Locke (1985, 140) studied this place, there was an image of Akṣobhya inside the middle shrine, an image of Prajñāpāramitā inside the shrine right to it and an image of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara inside the left shrine, however these images have since been stolen. In their place, statues of a doner in the act of praying have been installed inside the middle shrine, whilst the right-hand shirine now contains an image of Lakṣmī holding a lotus flower in her hand. The left-hand shrine has been furnished with an image of a two-handed Lokeśvara holding a lotus in his left hand and with his right hand in a varada gesture. Above the middle and the left shrine, one can find images of Mahākāla and three doners. These have been placed in a disorganized way. Local people claim that this Bāhāḥwas made by Śreṣṭhas. Apart from this, nothing more is known about its history. 

Inside the courtyard, there is one śikharakūṭa caitya and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala. At the eastern corner of the courtyard is a bell that was donated in NS 1049, and at the southern corner one can find another small caitya. Note that the illustration identified by Locke (1985, 141I) as Ikhalakhu Baha is actually Iku Baha, and the photograph of Ikhalaku (mis-labeled as Iku Baha) is actually on p. 139.

_source.displaydescription:
Vãlā Bāhāḥ, a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440), is located to the east of Pūrṇacandī Temple and to the north of the street that leads to Ikhālakhu. The bāhāḥ can be accessed by turning left down a narrow alleyway. It is called a bāhāḥ or vihāra even though it lacks a kvāḥpāḥchẽ. A small shrine of the bāhāḥ is attached to the southern wall of the courtyard. The wooden carved door of the sanctum is surmounted by a toraṇa displaying an image of Vajrasattva. However, Locke (1985, 169) identifies the deity as Akṣobhya. Inside the sanctum, one can find a north-facing stone image of Akṣobhya. There are two small niches on either side of the shrine. According to Vajrācārya (1993, 134) there was once an image of Mahākāla in the western niche. However, this is now missing.

The main temple structure is built on a double plinth. A stone threshold on the upper plinth provides the base for the carved wooden structure, which is open at three sides and has a rear boundary wall for support. The structure has two tiers of cement roof and a bell-shaped stūpa as its finial. Ten struts support the roof. There is a dharmadhātu jinālaya caitya in front of the main shrine.

Hela Thakuṃ built this bāhāḥ in 1921 (NS 1041) in memory of her late son Harṣavīra Vajrācārya. He was the eldest son of Dhīrjavīra Kampanī, a famous devotee and donor living in Dhyākva Nhūchẽ Kavaḥ of Bu Bāhāḥ. A ceremony called vãlā was organised on the inauguration day of the bāhāḥ, during which a procession passed through the main bāhās and bahīs of Patan. This bāhāḥ is named after the procession (Vajrācārya 1933, 134).

Three branches of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ are located in Chāḥ Bāhāḥ ṭola. All of these branches are known as Chāḥ Bāhāḥ and so it is unclear which one is actually the Chāḥ Bāhāḥ.

This Bāhāḥ is also called Bāhāḥcā in reference to its small size. It is located ca. 65 meters east of the Chāya Bāhāḥ Hiti. The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ can be reached by passing through a narrow alley and a carved door. The small courtyard measures 620 cm x 445 cm and houses an octagonal aṣṭakoṇaparivṛtākāra caitya. The main entrance to the Bāhāḥ is through a carved door, though there is also a plain door and a lattice window on its ground floor. Six statues flank the main door, with Khyāka, Gaṇeśa and Sāriputra to the left and Kavã, Mahākāla and Maudgalyāyana to the right. The statues of Khāka and Kavã are an interesting addition to this Buddhist monastic building, as they are more commonly found in the Śākta temples of the Valley. A pair of three praying wheels are fixed above the statues, and a wooden toraṇa with the images of Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara is fixed above the door. 

The Bāhāḥcā has a cement-plastered façade and a pāsukhā jhyāḥ on its first floor. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in its sanctum and an aniconic stone attached to the left wall of the building is worshipped as Bhairava.

Relying on an inscription, Locke (1985, 44) dates the Bāhāḥ to NS 779 (1659 CE). A completely effaced stone inscription is attached to the wall of the building and is likely the one that Locke used for this. Four families take care of the Bāhāḥ, performing its daily ritual worships and other social-religious activities.
